title: Corporate Finance — The Cash Conversion Cycle and the Cost of Forgoing a Trade Discount
scenario: Lakeshore Foods has annual sales of $146,000,000. Its current operating statistics show days sales outstanding of 52 days, days inventory on hand of 68 days, and days payables outstanding of 35 days. The treasurer believes a collections and warehouse initiative can shorten the cash conversion cycle by 15 days. Lakeshore borrows on its revolving line at 9%. Separately, its largest ingredient supplier has offered credit terms of 2/10, net 45, and Lakeshore currently pays on day 45 without taking the discount. Use a 365-day year. Answer each requirement in complete sentences and show your computations.

data.currentPaymentPractice: pays on day 45, discount not taken

requirements.prompt: Requirement 1 — Compute the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle. Then compute the cash that a 15-day reduction would release and the annual interest saving if that cash retires borrowings on the revolver, and explain what the cash conversion cycle measures.

noneOf: the cash conversion cycle is 120 days
cash conversion cycle equals the operating cycle

requirements.modelAnswer: The operating cycle is days inventory plus days receivable, 68 plus 52, which is 120 days. Subtracting the 35 days Lakeshore takes to pay suppliers leaves a cash conversion cycle of 85 days. Sales of $146,000,000 over 365 days are $400,000 a day, so removing 15 days of the cycle releases 15 times that amount, or $6,000,000 of cash. Applied against the revolver at 9%, that saves $540,000 of interest a year. The cycle measures how long a dollar stays trapped between paying a supplier and collecting from a customer, and every day of it must be financed by someone. Shortening the cycle is therefore a source of funding that costs nothing to raise, which is why it usually beats negotiating a slightly better rate on the line.

requirements.prompt: Requirement 2 — Compute the annualized cost of forgoing the 2/10, net 45 discount on both a nominal and an effective annual basis, recommend whether Lakeshore should take the discount, and explain the risk of funding working capital by stretching payables instead.

noneOf: borrowing to take the discount is uneconomic
the discount is not worth financing

requirements.modelAnswer: Forgoing the discount means paying 2% more to keep the money an extra 35 days, from day 10 to day 45. The nominal annualized cost is 2 divided by 98, which is 2.04%, multiplied by 365 over 35, giving 21.3%. Compounding that same periodic rate 10.43 times a year raises the effective annual cost to about 23.5%. Against a revolver that costs 9%, the comparison is not close, so Lakeshore should take the discount and fund the earlier payment by borrowing on the revolver. Stretching payables looks free but is not: suppliers eventually price the delay into quotes, shorten terms, deprioritize the account during shortages, and report slow payment to trade credit agencies. For a food processor dependent on ingredient availability, that supplier relationship is worth more than the float.
